newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS - Steelmakers optimistic about prices, demand.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Steelmakers optimistic about prices, demand.

text.p: World steelmakers on Monday spoke optimistically of improving steel prices, long in the doldrums, and they confidently projected solid demand trends for this year and next.

"I think we have hit the bottom. We expect prices to improve in the coming months," said Kim Mahn Je, chairman of the world's second biggest steel producer, South Korean Pohang Iron & Steel Co Ltd (POSCO).

"In the U.S. prices have been recovering ahead of other markets (and) Europe is following suit," Kim told a Reuter reporter on the opening day of the annual congress of the International Iron and Steel Institute (IISI) here.
"Prices in Japan are rising slowly, and we hope Korea will follow," he added.
U.S. steel producers also saw prices on the mend, though Bethlehem Steel Corp chairman and CEO Curtis Barnette said inflation-adjusted prices still lagged behind the 1995 level.
"There has been an improvement (in steel prices), but 1996 pricing is not yet back to the 1995 level," Barnette said. "Steel is a bargain in terms of affordability," he said.
European steel industry leaders have also voiced optimism that prices in Europe may have bottomed out.
Finnish steel group Rautaruukki Oy's president and CEO Mikko Kivimaki said on Saturday he was optimistic about the price outlook in Europe.
"In hot and cold rolled products, prices have reached the bottom," Kivimaki told a weekend news conference ahead of the IISI conference and added: "But I am very optimistic."
In galvanised and coated steel products, "the price increase has already picked up," Kivimaki said.
With steel prices firming, steelmakers said demand also looked solid.
The IISI predicted on Monday that world consumption of steel products will rise 3.4 percent to reach a record 680 million tonnes in 1997.
It said 1996 consumption was expected to total 657 million tonnes, five million tonnes over the 1995 level.
The steelmakers' organisation said strong housing starts and automotive sales in the United States would keep demand there around 100 million tonnes this year.
In the European Union, it said average economic growth would be below two percent, largely due to restrictions being imposed to meet the criteria for joining the single European currency.

"It is now widely believed that (steel) inventories are back to normal levels, and the absence of their negative effect in 1997, together with real growth in steel use, means that apparent consumption next year in the European Union will rise by 5.7 million tonnes, or five percent," it said.

Steel consumption in central and eastern Europe has however slowed and after a jump of more than 20 percent in 1995, steel consumption is expected to rise only by 2.9 percent and 2.5 percent in 1996 and 1997, taking the area's steel consumption to 18.3 million tonnes next year.
In Russia, steel consumption would continue to shrink in 1996 and 1997. Russia consumes 17 million tonnes of steel annually and exports about 60 percent of its steel.

"Very little is known about the development of the steel market in the other republics of the former Soviet Union, but their combined consumption, including that of Russia, is estimated to be about 35 million tonnes," IISI said.

In China, the steel market has been burdened by high inventories which will hold apparent 1996 consumption to 95 million tonnes, IISI said. "However, the inventory rundown is now over and 1997 consumption will probably rise to 100 million tonnes".

In Japan, consumption will probably rise by about two percent in 1996 from 1995 but high inventories will dent apparent consumption: IISI said falling demand from construction in 1997 would cut apparent consumption by almost one percent, to 78.6 million tonnes.
Globablly in the medium term, IISI said that apart from cyclical variations it did not see much change in the volume of steel consumption in the mature industrial markets.
It forecast an overall 1.8 percent increase in consumption to 714 million tonnes in 2000 from 652.2 million tonnes in 1995.

Growth would continue in developing regions, particularly in South America and China, IISI said, but added there were signs of maturity and slowing growth in the big Asian economies of Korea and Taiwan.
